content: Alisma plantago-aquatica, commonly referred to as the Common Water-plantain or Mad-dog weed, is a flowering plant that is native to a wide range of regions across the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, northern Asia, and North America. This plant typically thrives in shallow water environments. It is characterized by a fibrous root system, several basal leaves that measure between 15 to 30 cm in length, and a triangular stem that can grow up to 1 meter tall. The plant produces a branched inflorescence that bears numerous small flowers. These flowers have three rounded or slightly jagged petals, which are either white or pale purple in color. The name Alisma is believed to have Celtic origins, meaning water, which reflects the aquatic habitat in which the plant is commonly found. Early botanists named it after the plantain (Plantago) due to the resemblance between their leaves. The dried leaves of the Common Water-plantain have been traditionally used for medicinal purposes. They function as both a diuretic, promoting the excretion of urine, and a diaphoretic, inducing perspiration. These properties have made the plant useful in the treatment of conditions such as renal calculus (kidney stones), cystitis (inflammation of the bladder), dysentery, and epilepsy. Historically, the roots of the plant were used as a remedy for hydrophobia (rabies) and were reputed in America to be effective in treating rattlesnake bites.
